Asi usually denotes the sacrificial knife, but occasionally appears to mean a knife used in war. Mention is made of a sheath (vavri) to which a belt (vāla) was attached. The word asi-dhārā also denotes ‘sheath.’
Foot notes Rv. i. 162, 20; x. 79, 6; 18; Av. ix. 3, 9; x. 1, 20, etc.
Av. xi. 9, 1. The use of the ‘sword’ increases in the Epic period. See Hopkins, Journal of the American Oriental Society, 13, 284.

Asiknī (‘black’) is the name in the Rigveda of the river known later as candra-bhāgā, and to the Greeks as Akesines, now the Chenab in the Punjab.
Foot notes viii. 20, 25; x. 75, 5; nirukta, ix. 26. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 12.

1. Asita is a name of the ‘black snake,’ referred to in the later Saṃhitās.
Foot notes Av. iii. 27, 1; v. 13, 5. 6; vi. 56, 2, etc.; taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 10, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 18; perhaps Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 37.

2. Asita.--(a) A mythical sage of this name figures as a magician in the Atharvaveda in conjunction with gaya or with jamadagni. In the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa he appears as asita dhānva, and as daivala or devala in the Pañcaviṃsa brāhmaṇa and kāṭhaka Saṃhitā.
(b) asita vārṣa-gaṇa is a pupil of harita kaśyapa according to the vaṃśa or Genealogy in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad.
Foot notes Av. i. 14, 4.

Asita-mṛga is the designation in the aitareya brāhmaṇa of a family of the Kaśyapas who were excluded from a sacrifice by janamejaya, but who took away the conduct of the offering from the Bhūtavīras, whom the king employed. In the Jaiminīya brāhmaṇa and the Ṣaḍviṃsa brāhmaṇa the Asitamṛgas are called ‘sons of the Kaśyapas,’ and one is mentioned as Kusurubindu auddālaki.
Foot notes vii. 27. Cf. Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East, 43, 345.

Āśī-viṣa, occurring only in the aitareya brāhmaṇa, is understood by Roth as designating a particular kind of snake, and perhaps means ‘having poison (viṣa) in its fangs’ (āśī).
Foot notes vi. 1.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v. It is a common word in the Epic and later.
